pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–10, Natural resources — [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS3-1]; using them affects the environment; distinguish renewable (wind, solar, water) from non-renewable (fossil fuels) sources.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 science/geography — energy resources and their environmental impact; renewable vs non-renewable vocabulary (fossil fuel, carbon footprint, sustainability); builds on human-impact vocabulary.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 4-ESS3-1 (verbatim) — '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS3-1].' Clarification: renewable (wind, water behind dams, sunlight) vs non-renewable (fossil fuels, fissile materials); effects include habitat loss (dams, surface mining) and air pollution. DCI ESS3.A; SEP Obtaining/Evaluating/Communicating Information; CCC Cause & Effect. State/regional tier DEFERRED.
• Operational details: teach the renewable/non-renewable distinction (does it replenish on a human timescale?) and the environmental trade-offs of each source; the SEP is information-gathering-and-combining, so build from comparing real sources of information about impacts; connect fossil-fuel CO₂ forward to Climate Change Basics.
• Checkpoint (Tier A|B|C): Tier A — name energy resources and sort renewable vs non-renewable; Tier B — describe how extracting/using a resource affects the environment; Tier C — weigh trade-offs across sources using combined information.
bestPractices: Anchor the renewable/non-renewable distinction on replenishment timescale (renews within a human lifetime vs effectively finite)
Make environmental effects concrete per source (fossil-fuel air pollution + CO₂; dam habitat loss; mining habitat loss) rather than 'renewables good, others bad'
Honour the 4-ESS3-1 practice — have children OBTAIN and COMBINE information from more than one source to describe impacts
Surface trade-offs (renewables are clean but weather-dependent and land-hungry; fossil fuels are dense but polluting and finite)
Bridge forward to climate change (fossil-fuel CO₂) so the environmental effect has a named consequence
keyRepresentations: A renewable vs non-renewable sorting mat
Per-source cards showing origin, cost, environmental effect and whether it depletes
An energy-mix / 'power the town' balance with consequence readouts
Cause-and-effect chains from resource use to environmental impact
commonMisconceptions: Renewable simply means 'clean with no downsides' — renewables have impacts too (land use, dam habitat loss, intermittency)
Fossil fuels will 'never run out' or renew quickly — they form over millions of years and are effectively finite
Electricity is itself a fuel/resource — it is a carrier generated from a primary resource
Any environmentally friendly choice fixes every problem at once
Nuclear is 'renewable' — fissile material is a non-renewable resource

learn.summary: For ages 9–10 (NGSS 4-ESS3-1): energy and fuels come from natural resources, and using them affects the environment. Children distinguish renewable sources (wind, solar, water behind dams) from non-renewable ones (fossil fuels, fissile materials) using the replenishment-timescale criterion, and weigh the environmental trade-offs of each. The target science practice is obtaining and combining information from more than one source, so the strongest work has learners compare real information about impacts rather than accept 'renewables good, others bad'. Activities span an energy-mix decision bench, an in-role debate that exercises combining evidence, and a sorting/matching classification check.

activities.title: Power your town: an energy-mix decision bench
feedback: If the town runs out of power after switching off fossil fuels: notice that wind and solar make no air pollution while running but are weather-dependent and land-hungry, so you needed many more units. This is the trade-off, not a reason to call them 'bad'.
If a learner treats renewables as having no downside: point to the dam flooding a valley and the number of wind/solar units needed — land use and intermittency are real impacts.
If the coal fuel bar drains to empty: that draining is the point — fossil fuels are finite because they formed over millions of years and are not replaced in a human lifetime.

If a learner assumes switching to renewables fixes every environmental problem at once: note that each source still has its own footprint (land, materials, habitat), so no single switch solves everything — the aim is weighing trade-offs, not finding one perfect option.
activities.rationale: Letting consequences (pollution, depletion, land/habitat impact) respond to each allocation makes the renewable/finite distinction and the trade-offs concrete, and supports the 4-ESS3-1 emphasis on cause-and-effect reasoning about resource use. The live readouts (fuel bars draining, air greying, unit counts) are suggested illustrative mechanisms, not required ones; a paper or spoken version can carry the same reasoning.
sourceClaims: NGSS 4-ESS3-1 (verbatim): '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS3-1].' Clarification: renewable examples wind, water behind dams, sunlight; non-renewable are fossil fuels and fissile materials; environmental effects include habitat loss from dams and surface mining and air pollution from burning fossil fuels. DCI ESS3.A; SEP Obtaining/Evaluating/Communicating Information; CCC Cause and Effect. No assessment boundary listed.
Renewable resources replenish on a human timescale while fossil fuels form over millions of years and are effectively finite; all sources carry some environmental trade-off.
learnerActions: Allocate an energy mix to keep a town's lights on, dragging in options such as coal, gas, wind, solar and hydro to meet demand.

Watch each choice's consequences update: a coal plant gives steady power, but the sky greys with smoke pollution, invisible CO₂ builds up, and its fuel bar drains toward empty; wind and solar make no air pollution while running but need many units and sag when the weather turns or (for solar) at night; a dam delivers fairly steady power but floods a valley.
Switch the town fully off fossil fuels and observe what changes — the air clears and the fuel gauges stop draining, but far more renewable capacity is needed and output dips with the weather.
State in your own words which sources refill on a human timescale and which run out, and name one environmental trade-off for each source you used.
activities.intendedInsight: Renewable vs non-renewable is about whether the source refills on a human timescale, and every source carries an environmental trade-off rather than being simply 'good' or 'bad'.

activities.title: Obtain and combine: energy-engineer debate
feedback: If a learner relies on a single source: push them to find a second source and say what it adds or contradicts.
If a learner's recommendation ignores downsides: ask what the environmentalist (or the engineer) would raise against it, then revise.
Good justifications connect the choice to a named environmental effect, e.g. fossil-fuel CO₂ linked forward to climate change.
activities.rationale: The specified science practice is obtaining and combining information; constructing an argument in role requires learners to produce reasoning from combined evidence rather than only recognise it. Role/debate is proposed as one way to exercise this and is not claimed to be uniquely effective compared with other media.

Clarification: renewable examples wind, water behind dams, sunlight; non-renewable are fossil fuels and fissile materials; environmental effects include habitat loss from dams and surface mining and air pollution from burning fossil fuels. DCI ESS3.A; SEP Obtaining/Evaluating/Communicating Information; CCC Cause and Effect. No assessment boundary listed.
learnerActions: Take the role of an energy engineer, or hold a debate between an energy-company voice and an environmentalist, and gather information about a chosen energy source from more than one source of information.
Combine the information to describe how extracting and using that source affects the environment (for example fossil-fuel air pollution and CO₂, dam or mining habitat loss).
Justify a recommended resource choice by its environmental effects, acknowledging at least one downside of the option you favour.
activities.intendedInsight: The 4-ESS3-1 practice is obtaining and combining information from multiple sources and weighing competing evidence to justify a position about resource use.

activities.title: Sort and match: renewable, non-renewable, and their impacts
feedback: If nuclear is sorted as renewable: fissile material is finite, so it is non-renewable even though a reactor emits little CO₂ during operation.
If electricity is listed as a resource: electricity is carried energy generated FROM a primary resource, not a resource itself.
If a learner equates renewable with 'zero impact': renewables are lower-carbon but still have footprints (land, materials, dam habitat loss, intermittency).
If a learner classifies by 'makes electricity': classification is about replenishment, not about what the source powers — both wind and coal can generate electricity.
activities.rationale: A categorise-plus-match check maps directly onto the evidence statements and surfaces the specific misconceptions (nuclear-as-renewable, electricity-as-resource, renewable-as-electricity, renewable-as-impact-free). Recognition items check sorting but do not by themselves show independent construction, so pair this with the debate activity.
sourceClaims: Common misconceptions include treating renewables as impact-free, believing fossil fuels won't run out, classing nuclear as renewable, and treating electricity as a primary fuel.
Renewable resources replenish on a human timescale while fossil fuels form over millions of years and are effectively finite; all sources carry some environmental trade-off.
learnerActions: Sort energy resources (coal, oil, gas, wind, sun, water) into renewable vs non-renewable using the replenishment criterion.
Match each resource to its characteristic environmental effect (e.g. burning fossil fuels → air pollution and CO₂; dams → habitat loss by flooding; surface mining → habitat loss).
Decide the two tricky classification cases: whether nuclear/fissile material is renewable, and whether electricity is a primary resource.
Given a new source not practised, classify it by whether it refills on a human timescale.
activities.intendedInsight: Renewable/non-renewable is defined by whether the resource naturally replenishes on a human timescale, which is separate from how clean it is and separate from electricity (a carrier, not a resource).

constraints: Define renewable/non-renewable by replenishment timescale: renewable sources are replenished within a human lifetime, while non-renewable ones are not replenished on human timescales. Fossil fuels take millions of years to form, and fissile uranium is not naturally replenished on Earth at all. Do not define them by cleanliness or by whether a source generates electricity.

Keep environmental effects concrete and source-specific (fossil-fuel air pollution and CO₂; dam habitat loss from flooding; mining habitat loss) and avoid a blanket 'renewables good, everything else bad' message; renewables carry land-use and intermittency trade-offs.
Treat nuclear/fissile material as non-renewable and electricity as an energy carrier, not a primary resource.

The sorting/matching check verifies classification but does not by itself elicit the obtain-and-combine practice; use the debate/engineer task for independent construction of argument from multiple sources.

The energy-mix bench's live readouts (fuel bars, air colour, unit counts) are illustrative feedback mechanisms, not mandatory implementations; a paper or spoken version can carry the same trade-off reasoning.
Bridge fossil-fuel CO₂ forward to climate change so the environmental effect has a named consequence, but do not overstate that any single 'green' choice fixes every problem at once.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source's artefact rationales asserted that 'a static image can't let the child feel the trade-offs' and that role/debate works 'in a way a fixed artefact can't'. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited sources; they have been softened to scoped proposals noting affordances (live/responsive feedback, independent construction) rather than universal medium superiority.

Two of the three sources (EIA/Met Office energy education; energy-education misconception literature) are marked verified:false in the row; the replenishment-timescale and misconception claims should be confirmed against primary materials before relying on them as established fact.

The non-preferred 'tap each resource to reveal origin/impact' reference artefact was not carried as a standalone activity; its reference-card content is folded into the sort/match activity. If a low-stakes browse-and-reveal reference is wanted, it can be reinstated as a scaffold preceding the decision bench.

probeDeeper: Sunlight and coal both give us energy. Why will one still be here in a million years and the other might be gone?
Is a solar farm completely harmless to the environment? What might its downside be?
How does burning coal, oil or gas actually change the environment?
assess.correctAnswer: Wind is renewable, coal is non-renewable. Renewable means the resource is naturally replenished on a human timescale and won't run out from use (wind, sunlight, flowing water); non-renewable means there's a finite amount that took millions of years to form and gets used up (coal, oil, gas). Renewable doesn't mean 'no environmental impact,' but non-renewable fossil fuels release CO₂ and pollution when burned.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Renewable means it makes electricity; non-renewable means it doesn't'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Renewable is about the resource being naturally replaced, not about what it powers.
errorPatterns.distractor: Renewable resources are the ones that make electricity.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: classifies by whether it powers electronics, not by replenishment

errorPatterns.pattern: No sense of finite, million-year formation — can't say why coal/oil run out
errorPatterns.nextMove: They formed from ancient organisms over millions of years and can't be remade in time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: treats fossil fuels as easily replaceable

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Renewable energy has no effect on the environment at all'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Renewables are lower-carbon but still have footprints (land, materials); the key contrast is finite + CO₂ from burning.
errorPatterns.distractor: Renewable energy sources have no environmental impact whatsoever.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Electricity itself is a fuel / a natural resource'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Electricity is carried energy, made FROM a resource — not a resource itself.

responseLevels.gap: Classifies sources by whether they make electricity, or can't tell renewable from non-renewable.
responseLevels.full: Names resources, classifies by the naturally-replenished/finite criterion, and describes environmental effects — distinguishing lower-impact renewables from CO₂-emitting fossil fuels and transferring to a new source.
responseLevels.partial: Sorts renewable vs non-renewable correctly and names resources but can't explain the replenishment criterion, or equates renewable with zero environmental impact.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Wind turbines and coal power stations both make electricity. One uses a renewable resource and one a non-renewable resource. Which is which — and what does 'renewable' actually mean about that resource?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks 'renewable = electric' or 'renewable = zero impact' mislabels sources; only a child using the runs-out / naturally-replenished criterion classifies correctly and separates that from environmental impact.
